newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Promise of Brazil retail banking draws foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Promise of Brazil retail banking draws foreigners.

text.p: The purchase of Banco Noroeste by Spain's Banco Santander highlights the rising interest of foreign banks in Brazil's appealing retail banking market, bank analysts said.

Noroeste, a mid-sized bank focusing on individuals and smaller corporate clients, was Santander's second acquisition in Brazil, allowing it to expand its local network and client base to better compete in consumer banking, they said.
In March, Santander bought a controlling stake in Banco Geral do Comercio, which it used to buy 50 percent of Noroeste for an estimated $500 million.

"The steps taken by Santander in acquiring two banks here confirm the interest of big foreign retail banks in Latin America and Brazil in particular," said Carlos Daniel Coradi, director at EFC banking consulting firm.

Santander's purchase of Noroeste was just the latest foreign acquisition of a Brazilian bank. The first big investment was made by HSBC Holdings Plc, which early this year took over failed retail bank Banco Bamerindus.

Analysts said the Santander deal underlines the huge growth potential of Brazil's retail banking sector as the country's recent economic stability has led to increasing demand for credit and financial services products.
"Banking loans are still very low in Brazil, when compared with gross domestic product. Banks have a lot of room to grow in financing," said Antonio Madeira, analyst at MCM consulting firm.
Analysts believe the acquisitions by HSBC and Santander are just the start of a wave of foreign takeovers of Brazilian banks. "I have no doubt that other retail banks will come," Coradi said.
But foreign banks will not likely dominate Brazil's retail banking sector as they did in Argentina, where only one major bank remains in local hands.

Analysts said mid-sized Brazilian banks are likely to be the channel through which foreigners will enter the Brazilian market because they need larger partners to survive in an increasingly competitive market.
"There are still medium-sized banks which need to join forces with bigger institutions to grow to compete," said Renato Pinto, an analyst at Caspian Securities in Brazil.
Brazil's state bank privatization drive also opens opportunities to foreigners, bank analysts said.

At least two state-owned banks -- Meridional and Banespa -- are likely to attract institutions from overseas, they said. So far only two state banks have been privatized, Banerj and Credireal, but they were bought by other Brazilian banks.
